text: Conditional Access doesn't have a concept of Azure resources versus everything else. It evaluates a sign-in — who the user is, whether their device reports as compliant, where they're signing in from, and what Identity Protection's risk engine thinks of the attempt — and then decides whether to allow it, block it, or demand MFA before access to a specific target application is granted.

The fact that makes this lesson possible: once AWS IAM Identity Center is set up as a SAML enterprise application in your Entra ID tenant, it is a target application in exactly the sense Conditional Access already understands. A policy that targets Office 365 or SharePoint Online can target AWS IAM Identity Center the identical way — no second product to learn, no separate AWS-side access concept.

That's why the better move is extending the policy you already trust instead of writing a parallel one. Open the rule requiring a compliant device, phishing-resistant MFA, and a block on legacy authentication, and add AWS IAM Identity Center to its target apps. Now there's exactly one rule enforced in one place — tighten it once, and both Microsoft and AWS sign-ins move together instead of drifting apart.

The signals worth leaning on here are device compliance through Intune, phishing-resistant MFA for anyone with admin-level permission sets, sign-in risk from Identity Protection, and named locations. One real limit to know: Conditional Access evaluates the sign-in itself, not every AWS API call afterward — AWS doesn't ask Entra ID's permission for every S3 request once STS credentials exist.

What you control instead is how often the session has to come back through Entra ID to refresh, using sign-in frequency on the policy. Shorter frequency means a stale or risky session gets re-evaluated sooner — the practical substitute for continuous checking on a third-party relying party like AWS. Next lesson pulls this whole chapter together.
